arbitrated.notes:
Labour is loosening clearly. The unemployment rate has fallen from 5.5% to 4.9% over twelve months and stands just 0.1 pp above its 12-month low, but recent momentum has stalled—flat over three months and the last two prints show slight upticks to 5.0% and 4.9%. The 3-month average sits at 4.9%, a 0.2 pp decline from six months ago, suggesting labour has cooled from even recent levels. Most tellingly, the Sahm rule gap is barely positive at +0.10 pp, a signal that historically precedes recessions; the rate sits 0.90 pp above estimated natural rate but that gap has narrowed sharply. Labour is visibly loosening.

Inflation, by contrast, remains unsettled despite a confusing near-term picture. Headline CPI has spiked to 0.85% year-on-year from 0.64% last month, a volatile series gyrating between -0.10% and +1.24% over the past year. The three-month annualized headline pace is deeply negative at -1.14%, yet the outgoing month-on-month read is +0.27%, suggesting base effects may be distorting signals. Core PCE—the Fed's preferred measure—accelerated to 1.41% from 1.19%, now only 0.59 pp below the 2% target, a material tightening of slack. Core has moved +0.23 pp over three months, and the momentum in core-minus-headline at +0.56 pp shows service-price inflation persisting. The inflation panel lacks clarity because headline swings mask the stickier core signal: disinflationary pressure is real but core remains stubbornly above target.

Given the reaction function, labour loosening normally demands rate cuts. But core inflation is still elevated, the Fed is closer to its 2% target than the panic in headline suggests, and the Fed does not cut into core at 1.41% with labour only moderately soft. The near-term path should price cuts only if labour continues to deteriorate sharply or if core drops to 1.2% or below. Right now, the Fed likely pauses and waits; this panel does not yet call for tightening but it does not yet call for cuts either.

Financial conditions have tightened marginally—the NFCI has drifted from -0.44 to -0.28 over the past year, a +0.17 index rise, and now sits firmly in its upper-half range position at 0.96. Conditions remain accommodative but the trend is toward restraint. The Fed's balance sheet has grown modestly—assets are up $12.7B over 13 weeks and $3.1B over the year—which is broadly neutral and not a constraint. Conditions are tightening gently but neither financial stress nor fresh monetary accommodation is the story.

trade.rationale: Labour loosening calls for duration long, but core inflation still elevated argues against steep cuts near term. Sell 2y and buy 3m to flatten the front end—betting on patience, not cuts. Position reflects pause, not tightening.

Labour loosening has emerged as the clearest signal in the panel. Unemployment has compressed into the 4.7–4.9% range over the last three months, with a three-month change of -20bp and a 12-month low now sitting at 4.7%. The unemployment rate is currently at its 12-month low, and the Sahm gap is flat at zero, meaning there is no recession signal from labour. However, the rate sits 70bp above the estimated natural rate, leaving material slack on the supply side. This is a labour market that is neither tight nor loose in absolute terms, but the trajectory is one of gradual loosening from a position that was not far above trend.

Inflation, by contrast, is accelerating sharply and has become the live issue. Headline CPI year-on-year has jumped from 1.68% to 2.51% in just three observations—an 83bp three-month rise—and is now at the top of its 52-week range. The month-on-month momentum is even more concerning: at 0.40% m/m (the hottest observation in the panel), it sits 39bp above the outgoing level and well above the three-month average. The headline 3m annualized print is 3.14%, a materially hot clip. Core PCE, though less alarming at 1.86% y/y, is also rising: it has moved +8bp over three months and sits only 14bp below the Fed's 2% target. This is an inflation picture where the recent move is real, not noise.

Financial conditions have loosened measurably. The NFCI sits at -0.49, its 52-week low, with a 13-week tightening of -12bp. This is accommodation, not constraint. The Fed's balance sheet has shrunk 29.5bn over 52 weeks but is currently stable at the margin (+1.4bn over four weeks), and the recent level is near the mid-point of the recent trading range.

The reaction function tension here is real but resolvable. Labour is loosening, but inflation is accelerating *now*—and the Fed weights the inflation signal more heavily once it moves this sharp and this recent. The market should price less near-term Fed tightening because the central bank faces a dilemma: the labour market is already supplying some disinflationary pressure (loosening), while inflation momentum is hot enough to demand policy attention. The Fed will not cut immediately, but the path of hikes should flatten relative to what would be priced if inflation were merely sticky at high levels. The baseline is a hold into the next meeting(s), not further hikes.

{"notes": "Labor tightness has eased notably. The unemployment rate has fallen to 4.4% and sits 40bp below the natural rate estimate, but the directional signal is unmistakable: -40bp over 12 months, -30bp over 6 months, and -20bp over 3 months show a trend of loosening in the stock of joblessness. The Sahm gap is at zero, indicating no recession warning but also no exceptional tightness. The recent momentum — the last three prints all at 4.4% — suggests stabilization rather than further deterioration. This argues for less near-term Fed tightening.

Inflation is cooling but not collapsed. Headline CPI yoy has compressed from 2.81% to 1.86% in three months, a drop of 95bp. Core PCE has fallen from 1.87% to 1.55%, down 32bp in three months. Both are now below the 2% target. The 3-month annualized headline print is flat, and core is only 98bp annualized, but the monthly momentum is mixed: the last month showed a -8bp headline move after an outgoing +28bp. This suggests inflation is no longer a binding constraint on the reaction function, and the recent overshooting to the downside in headline raises the risk of policy overstay if the Fed does not adjust. The core-minus-headline gap at -31bp implies stable disinflation without breakdown in service inflation.

Financial conditions have tightened slightly: NFCI has drifted from -0.50 to -0.54 over 13 weeks, now at its 52-week low. This matters as a constraint — tighter conditions normally curb the need for additional policy tightening — but the change is marginal and the level remains accommodative. The Fed balance sheet has expanded $2.15B over 13 weeks, a trivial 5bp in percentage terms, reflecting recent QT pauses and Fed liquidity operations. This is not a loosening signal; it is stabilization at a very lean balance sheet.

arbitrated.notes:
Labour markets are cooling steadily but not sharply. Unemployment has drifted lower over the year—down 70bp—but recent momentum has flattened; the 3m change is only -10bp and the latest reading at 4.2% sits just 20bp above the estimated natural rate. The Sahm gap is negligible. This is a tight labour market that is slowly normalizing, not one in acute decompression. The path suggests the Fed can pause comfortably without labour becoming a fresh pressure driver over the next few months.

Inflation is the more live tension. Headline CPI sits at 2.02% yoy but has reaccelerated—up 30bp over the last three months on a yoy basis and running at 3.96% annualized on a 3m basis. Core PCE is anchored around target at 1.54% but also shows slight upside drift. Month-on-month momentum in headline is elevated (0.51% m/m most recently, well above the 0.12% outgoing rate), suggesting near-term price pressures have not fully unwound. The core-minus-headline spread remains wide and negative, reflecting energy and goods volatility, but the 3m annualized core rate of 1.92% is not alarming. The inflation panel shows a market still oscillating between disinflationary hope and renewed momentum; the reacceleration this quarter is material enough to keep the reaction function honest.

Financial conditions remain accommodative and stable well below zero. The balance sheet is in low-level drift—small recent inflows after 13w contraction—and exerts minimal constraint.

The near-term policy read: labour will not force the Fed's hand, but inflation's recent reacceleration means the tightening cycle is not over. The market should price the Fed on hold for now, but not price in the rate cuts a recent soft labour number might suggest. Core momentum is too sticky for that, and the monthly volatility in headline warns against anchoring to the headline level alone.
arbitrated.falsifier: A sharp drop in headline momentum (3m annualized dropping below 2.5%) or a significant miss-lower on the next CPI print, coupled with jobless claims acceleration, would suggest the Fed has already tightened enough.

Market positioning may already price the hold deeply; surprise pricing of continued tightening could whip yields if Powell sounds hawkish.
An unexpected labour weakness combined with stable inflation could push the Fed to pre-emptive cuts, shortening the hold.

The 3-month trend shows the rate holding just above that floor after a recent dip, suggesting labour markets remain tight but may be stabilising near peak tightness rather than continuing to loosen. This argues for pricing near-term rate cuts rather than holds or hikes.

Inflation presents a more complex picture. Headline CPI sits at 2.13% yoy, down 5bp over three months and well above the 12-month low of 1.64%. Core PCE at 1.58% is only 42bp below the Fed's 2% target and has reaccelerated 15bp over three months despite being lower than last year. The three-month annualized pace of core is 1.78%, suggesting modest underlying price pressure, while headline is 2.24% annualized. The momentum signal is ambiguous: last month's headline mom print was 0.40% (elevated), but the three-month average sits at a tame 0.18%, and the outgoing momentum of 0.40% exceeds the recent average by 22bp, hinting at near-term upside surprise risk.

Financial conditions remain accommodative at NFCI -0.61, unchanged at the 52-week low, offering no constraint. The Fed's balance sheet shows modest erosion (down 0.16% over 13 weeks, -2.8bn over the year), consistent with a slow, orderly wind-down; this is not tightening via the balance sheet.

The reaction-function tension is real: labour is tighter than inflation, but inflation remains above target and momentum is mixed. The labour tightness—being the clearer directional signal and the more forward-looking driver given the Sahm gap—should dominate the near-term path. The Fed is likely to be patient rather than aggressive, leaning toward cuts as labour slack opens, but inflation's stickiness and upside momentum risk argue against aggressive front-end flattening.

The unemployment rate sits at 3.8%, down 0.4pp over the past year, with the last three months flat at elevated levels within the 12-month range (3.7–4.2%). The Sahm rule gap is barely positive at +0.07pp, well short of recession territory. This tells me tightness is easing from overheated but remains above neutral—a labor market that no longer demands aggressive Fed tightening but hasn't triggered a rate-cut impulse either.

Inflation has cooled notably but sits above target and shows some stickiness. Headline CPI year-over-year has fallen 0.36pp over three months and now sits at 2.49%, but the recent month-on-month was 0.23%, and the 3-month annualized headline pace holds at 2.50%. Core PCE has drifted lower to 1.87% y/y, only 0.13pp above the Fed's target, but it too shows no clear downtrend recently (core 3-month annualized at 1.42% annualizes the recent stasis). The panel shows inflation on a slow glide but not yet at rest, especially for headline risk from energy or goods repricing.

Financial conditions remain accommodative (NFCI at −0.56, near the loose end of its 52-week range) and the Fed balance sheet is shrinking steadily (down 2.45% over 13 weeks), but neither is tightening hard enough to create a fresh policy constraint. Conditions are easing slightly at the margin (+0.03 4-week improvement), not tightening.

Together these inputs push toward a Fed holding rates steady in the near term. Labor no longer screams "tighten harder," inflation is cooling but not yet vindicated, and financial conditions pose no urgency to move. The front-end path should price patience: rates hold, not cuts, and not more hikes.

The three-month change of -0.20 pp and the 12-month drop of -0.40 pp confirm a tightening trend, though the pace has moderated in the last month (the rate bounced to 3.70% before returning to 3.60%). The Sahm gap is negligible and the distance from natural rate estimates suggests labor is still 40 bp tight. This is a live and material driver of near-term Fed policy, and the direction is clear: tighter labor, more tightening pressure.

Inflation has cooled substantially and is now running well below target. Headline CPI year-over-year stands at 1.67%, down 0.21 pp over three months, while core PCE has fallen to 1.56%, 0.18 pp lower over the same window. The three-month annualized rates paint a similar picture: headline at 1.48% and core at 1.59%, both benign. The recent monthly momentum is soft (headline mom at -0.03% last month, 0.08% the month before). Core sits 44 bp below the 2% target. This is a disinflationary read that removes urgency from Fed tightening and creates space for cuts, assuming labor does not re-tighten.

Financial conditions remain accommodative but have edged toward tightening. The NFCI sits at -0.57, only 0.02 index points looser than four weeks ago and 0.03 looser than 13 weeks ago. Labour has tightened unexpectedly in the past month, with the unemployment rate spiking from 3.5% to 4.4%. This sharp jump—the largest in the dataset—reverses six months of sub-3.6% readings and marks the highest level in over a year. The three-month change is now +0.80pp, the six-month change +0.90pp, and the twelve-month low sits at 3.5%, placing us at the extreme top of the observed range. The Sahm gap is positive but modest at +0.33pp, suggesting we are not yet in recession-signal territory, but the trajectory is unmistakably loosening. Near-term, this shift materially reduces the near-term tightening case the Fed has been running on.

Inflation, by contrast, shows sharp recent disinflation. Headline CPI has collapsed from 2.60% to 1.49% year-over-year—a move of -0.83pp in just three months—and is now at its lowest in the full year. The monthly momentum has turned sharply negative: last month's headline print was -0.45% m/m, far below the outgoing +0.38% pace. Core PCE is more stable, at 1.53% y/y, near the twelve-month low of 1.49%, and has barely moved in three months. The widening spread between headline and core reflects energy-driven disinflation, not pass-through. This is not a hot inflation backdrop; it is a cooling one.

Financial conditions have tightened materially over the past month and quarter, with the NFCI rising from -0.62 to +0.18 index—a +0.61 point move in four weeks and +0.72 in thirteen weeks. We are now at the top of the fifty-two-week range. This tightening in financial conditions is the mechanism through which the Fed's prior work is translating into real economic slack.

The Fed's balance sheet has expanded aggressively, with assets growing from ~4.2 trillion to 5.25 trillion in recent weeks—a +26% thirteen-week change. This reflects recent banking-system interventions and is a material loosening input, offsetting the tightening in financial conditions on the real economy.

The near-term reaction function is now dominated by labour loosening and disinflation, with financial conditions already doing the tightening work. The Fed's recent rate pause and forward guidance are consistent with this new regime. I see less room for further near-term tightening and material downside risk to the pricing if labour continues to soften.

Labour tightness has collapsed. The unemployment rate has surged 4.8 pp over the past year, from 3.6% to 8.4%, with the most violent move happening in the most recent month (spike to 10.2%–14.8% range visible in the data tail). The 3-month annualized change is -4.80 pp, the Sahm recession indicator sits at +6.37 pp, well into recessionary territory. The labour market is no longer tight; it is slack, and rapidly getting slacker. This is the dominant signal for the next month.

Inflation, however, tells a more complicated story. Headline CPI has rebounded sharply: the 3-month annualized rate is 5.61%, and the year-over-year momentum has risen 1.08 pp in the past three months, lifting headline from 0.20% to 1.28% y/y. Core PCE has also re-accelerated (3.27% annualized), with the 3-month y/y change of +0.40 pp pushing core to 1.39%. The most recent monthly reading (headline +0.37% m/m, well above the 0.15% outgoing) confirms the pickup is live. Yet core remains 0.61 pp below target, and both measures are still historically low in absolute terms.

The Fed faces a genuine dilemma. Traditional reaction functions weight labour deterioration very heavily—a Sahm spike of this magnitude would normally trigger urgent accommodation. But inflation has stopped falling and is now rising, albeit from depressed levels. The risk of continued disinflation has diminished; the risk of re-acceleration remains material.

Given the timing horizon (one month ahead), the labour deterioration will dominate the Fed's immediate reaction function, but it will be constrained by the need to monitor inflation momentum. The near-term path has room to shift from purely defensive to data-dependent, but a sharp turn to easing is not yet certain. Financial conditions remain loose, and the Fed balance sheet is stable, offering no additional constraint.

Inflation is nowhere near the 2016–2019 level, and the recent trajectory suggests disinflationary pressure dominates.

The near-term reaction function is now plainly driven by labour, not inflation. A labour market recovering firmly from shock, with momentum, faces an inflation regime already below target and disinflating. The Fed's next moves should price fewer cuts than the market may be priced for, but the direction of surprise is toward less tightening from here, not more. Labour tightness is unwinding. The unemployment rate has fallen to 6.2% over the last three months, but sits 2.2pp above estimated natural rates and 2.7pp above its 12-month low of 3.5%. The three-month change is -0.50pp but the twelve-month change is +2.70pp—the labour market has expanded significantly from its post-shock peak. The Sahm gap of +2.03pp signals slack has emerged. This is no longer a tight labour market; it is normalizing from abnormally tight conditions. The reaction function weights this heavily near-term.

Inflation is moving up at the front end. Headline CPI has risen from 0.20% (12 months back) to 1.67%, with the three-month annualized reading at 4.15%. Core PCE is at 1.70%, up from 0.97% a year ago, with three-month annualized at 2.97%. The outgoing month-on-month reading was -0.45%, but the three-month average is +0.34%, and the recent trend—0.24%, 0.43%, 0.34%—shows momentum. Core sits just 0.30pp below the 2% target. Near-term inflation risk is real and rising.

Financial conditions remain accommodative. The NFCI is at -0.62, unchanged from its 52-week low, stable over four weeks, with no signs of tightening. This is not a constraint.

The balance sheet is expanding. Fed assets have grown $373.6B over 13 weeks and $3.43T over the past year, positioning at the 52-week high. This is not restrictive; it is expansionary.

The front-end policy implication is clear: labour slack has emerged, removing the tightness constraint that dominated earlier in the cycle, while inflation is accelerating and remains above target. The Fed's reaction function will shift toward data-dependence on inflation, not labour tightness, over the near term. The market is not yet pricing enough near-term resilience of rates to inflation. A steepening within the front end is warranted.

Financial conditions remain accommodative but tightening gradually. The NFCI sits at –0.36, well below zero and only marginally away from its 52-week low of –0.44. arbitrated.notes: Labor is loosening gradually. The unemployment rate has drifted from 3.8% a year ago to 4.1% now, a thirty-basis-point increase over twelve months. Recent changes flatten that trend—no movement in the last three and six months—but the level remains above the 3.7% twelve-month low. The Sahm gap sits at 43 basis points, and the rate is now in the 80th percentile of its annual range. This points to a genuinely tighter labour market than the pre-pandemic trend, but momentum toward further loosening has stalled. Inflation remains sticky, though with a welcome recent pullback. Headline CPI has fallen from 3.49% a year ago to 2.87% now, and core PCE sits at 2.99%, just a point above the 2% target. Month-on-month readings have turned higher in recent weeks—the 3-month annualized headline is 3.70%—suggesting disinflation may not be finished. However, core-on-headline compression and the outgoing MoM at 0.31% imply the next print could soften. Financial conditions are accommodative and stable. The NFCI sits at -0.48, at the 52-week low (most accommodative), with negligible near-term movement. The Fed balance sheet is shrinking steadily—down $194 billion over thirteen weeks and $827 billion over the year—providing a modest restraining headwind as quantitative tightening proceeds. The reaction function must weigh these tensions: labour has stopped loosening and sits tight, inflation is sticky but trending the right direction, and conditions remain supportive. The market should price for the Fed to hold rates steady in the near term, perhaps indefinitely, given that both inflation and labour slack remain manageable and financial conditions pose no urgency to move. The balance sheet shrinkage is a slow constraint, not a catalyst for near-term rate moves.

arbitrated.notes:
The labour market shows early signs of loosening but remains close to equilibrium. The unemployment rate has fallen 10bp in three months and stands at 4.0%, down from a 12-month high of 4.2%, placing it at the lower end of recent range. The 12-month change of +30bp shows it has drifted up from pandemic lows, and the Sahm gap of +20bp is rising but still modest. There is no compelling evidence of imminent labour market weakness—the rate is stable, moves are small, and it sits roughly at estimated natural rate. For the reaction function, this is a constraint loosening gently but not yet forcing pivot.

Inflation remains the live driver. Headline CPI has re-accelerated sharply: the last two months averaged +0.39% m/m annualizing to 4.7%, and year-over-year has jumped 56bp in three months to 2.99%. Core PCE shows a softer picture (2.78% y/y, -21bp in three months), but this divergence reflects base effects, not disinflation durability. The three-month annualized headline momentum of 4.29% is high, and outgoing month-over-month inflation of +0.43% signals the next print could be sticky. Core remains 78bp above target and has not re-accelerated but has stabilized rather than continuing lower.

Financial conditions are accommodative—NFCI at -0.50 is at the 52-week low and has drifted easier over 13 weeks. The balance sheet continues to contract, down 2.78% over 13 weeks, but contraction is orderly and far below peak tightness.

The reaction function should weight labour as a modest constraint now but inflation as the binding driver in the near term. The Fed is unlikely to cut while headline inflation is accelerating and core stubbornly above target. The path is hold-steady, not cuts, until inflation cools more convincingly.

Supply-driven inflation surprises could push 2y yields sharply higher if data shocks hot repeatedly.

why.balance_sheet: Orderly 13w contraction of 2.78%; not a binding constraint on policy trajectory.

The Sahm gap, a near-recession indicator, now stands at +23bp—still below historical alarm thresholds but meaningful. The three-month change is modest at +10bp, suggesting the loosening is gradual rather than abrupt. This trajectory—slow, steady drift without a cliff—is consistent with a labour market normalizing from overheated levels rather than one in crisis.

Inflation remains sticky and elevated, though cooling off its recent highs. Headline CPI at 2.38% sits at the bottom of its 12-month range after a sharp 49bp three-month decline, but that decline masks volatility in month-on-month readings that have oscillated between -0.04% and +0.43%. Core PCE at 2.67% sits 67bp above the 2% target. The core-minus-headline spread of +29bp suggests services inflation is the persistent problem. The recent headline MoM of +0.22% and the outgoing number matching it suggest underlying momentum remains, not a durable break below trend.

Financial conditions have loosened slightly but remain accommodative in absolute terms, with the NFCI at -0.42 having crept back toward zero from -0.51 thirteen weeks ago. This is not a tightening constraint; it is marginal mean reversion within an easy regime. The Fed's balance sheet continues to shrink at a measured pace, with assets down 146bn over thirteen weeks and 744bn over the year—QT proceeding as planned without stress.

The live tension is between labour loosening and inflation stickiness. Labour is rolling over, but inflation has not yet broken decisively below target. The reaction function weights both, but the timing matters: if inflation is still 67bp above core target while labour is only marginally loose, the Fed is not yet in "can cut" territory. The current path prices more rate cuts than the data warrant. The reaction function still has to price the possibility that the Fed pauses or slows cuts if inflation reaccelerates, even as labour softens. {"notes": "The labour market shows unmistakable deterioration over a one-month horizon. Unemployment has risen 40 basis points over twelve months and now sits at 4.5%, the top of its recent range. The three-month change of +20bp and the Sahm gap of +40bp both signal loosening momentum. This shift from a tight labour market is material for the reaction function, though the level remains moderate and not recessionary.

Inflation presents a mixed picture. Headline CPI has edged back to 2.99% from a peak of 3.02%, and the core PCE deceleration over three months (−11bp) is constructive. However, both metrics remain elevated relative to the Fed's 2% target—core is 75bp above target, and headline's three-month annualized pace sits at 3.64%. The outgoing momentum readings are not falling cleanly: headline mom-on-mom remains sticky at 0.28-0.30%, conflicting with the year-over-year softening. This tension between backward-looking easing and forward-looking momentum risk leaves inflation as a constraint rather than a driver of further cuts.

Financial conditions are accommodative and stable. The NFCI sits at −0.50, well below zero, with only marginal tightening in recent weeks. This poses no near-term constraint on policy accommodation.

The Fed balance sheet continues its gradual normalization, down $35bn in four weeks and $52bn over thirteen weeks. At −77bp annualized over thirteen weeks, the shrinkage is orderly and predictable, supporting the case that QT is not a tightening shock to financial conditions.

The reaction function should pivot toward patience. arbitrated.notes: Labour is loosening moderately and should be the dominant near-term signal. The unemployment rate sits at 4.4%, having risen 0.4pp over twelve months and 0.1pp over six months, with a recent three-month decline of 0.1pp that fails to reverse the broader trend. The Sahm gap at +0.27pp and distance from natural rate at +0.4pp confirm the labour market is slack relative to cyclical peaks, even if not yet deeply loose. Core inflation remains elevated and sticky above target. Core PCE stands at 3.10% year-on-year—the highest observation in this panel and notably above the Fed's 2% target. The three-month annualized core rate at 3.86% is even hotter, reflecting recent momentum: core has risen 0.35pp over the past three months, while headline has declined 0.32pp. The headline mom at 0.27% is above the 0.23% outgoing rate, suggesting upside surprise risk. Financial conditions have actually tightened modestly over the past four weeks (+0.04 index on NFCI), though remain accommodative on an absolute basis at -0.52. The balance sheet is essentially flat in the near term, adding only $26B over four weeks and $61B over thirteen weeks—a meaningful deceleration from the $152B contraction over the past year. The combined read: labour slack is emerging and would normally support rate cuts, but core inflation is hotter than headlines suggest and refuses to roll over convincingly. The Fed's reaction function will weigh labour loosening as the primary argument for eventual cuts, but near-term policy will remain data-dependent on whether core moderates. The market should price a pause here, with cuts gradually priced in only as labour softens further and inflation gives clearer signs of mean reversion.
arbitrated.falsifier: Core PCE falls decisively below 2.5% annualized over next 6-8 weeks AND unemployment stays below 4.4%, signaling no slack—would flip to more tightening priced.

risks.text: Fed may remain hawkish longer if core stickiness is read as demand-driven and requires additional tightening before cuts begin.
A sharper labour softening than 0.4pp over 12m could accelerate cut expectations faster, steepening front end unexpectedly.
Market may have already priced significant labour loosening; trade crowded on cut expectations and vulnerable to inflation surprises.
If Fed pauses longer than expected, long-end yields could rise and steepen the curve, hurting the 2y long position.

trade.rationale: Labour loosening and inflation stickiness both argue against aggressive near-term tightening. Flatten front end: sell short rates (shorter duration support) and buy 2y, expecting curve to price in eventual cuts as slack widens but inflation caps terminal rate.

Labour market is loosening modestly but unevenly. The unemployment rate has drifted up 10 bps over the past year and ticked up 10 bps in the last three months, though the recent three-month average of 4.33% masks volatility—the rate swings between 4.30% and 4.40% in the latest observations. The Sahm gap sits at +0.23 pp, a level that historically signals early recession risk but not yet at the threshold where it dominates the Fed's reaction function. The labour market is still tight relative to its natural rate, estimated at 0.30 pp above neutral.

Inflation picked up sharply in the most recent month—headline CPI jumped to 3.32% y/y on a 0.87% m/m print, the highest in the series shown. Core PCE accelerated to 3.25% y/y, running 1.25 pp above the Fed's 2% target. Three-month annualized rates are hot: headline 5.33%, core 4.64%. The outgoing month-on-month is 0.03%, near the baseline, but the three-month average of 0.43% m/m is elevated, suggesting momentum. This is a material reversal from the soft-data regime of early readings.

Financial conditions have eased noticeably over the past four weeks (NFCI +0.06) and thirteen weeks (NFCI +0.06), lifting from -0.56 to -0.46. The index remains loose, but the trend is toward normalization. The Fed's balance sheet is expanding: assets have grown $43.4B in the past four weeks and $75.9B over thirteen weeks, though this represents only a +1.15% rise and remains $70.3B below the 52-week high. The policy emergency is past.

The near-term reaction function hinges on inflation momentum offsetting the early labour loosening signal. The Sahm gap warns but does not yet compel a pivot. The recent inflation spike is real, month-on-month intensity is elevated, and core remains stubbornly above target. For the next policy horizon, the market should expect the Fed to remain patient with rates at current levels, waiting for labour to deteriorate further or inflation to confirm a sustained decline. No fresh tightening is warranted, but a cut is not yet signalled either.

arbitrated.notes:
The near-term path is anchored to a labour market that is loosening modestly while inflation remains uncomfortably elevated. Unemployment has drifted sideways around 4.3%, with a three-month trend flat and a twelve-month trend up 0.1pp; the Sahm gap sits at +0.20pp and the market is 0.30pp above estimated natural rate. This is the signal of modest slack forming, not tight labour. Inflation, by contrast, is hot and accelerating. Headline CPI stands at 4.27% year-on-year, up 1.61pp over three months, while core PCE has risen to 3.41% and sits 1.41pp above the Fed's 2% target. Month-on-month momentum is elevated at 0.66% average over three months. The outgoing MoM at 0.10% is well below recent runs, but the recent hard print (0.87% in the penultimate month) signals the 3m annualized headline at 8.2% is material.

The Fed's near-term reaction function will weight this labour loosening against inflation persistence. The labour signal is real but incremental—not a warning sign of imminent recession, but permission to pause or slow further tightening. Inflation's near-term trajectory is the live constraint. At 1.41pp above target and accelerating, the Fed cannot yet declare victory and will resist the urge to cut ahead of clearer disinflation. Financial conditions remain easy (NFCI at -0.50, stable) and pose no constraint. The balance sheet has stabilized and grown modestly on the 13-week horizon, neither tightening nor loosening meaningfully.

The market should price less aggressive further tightening from here, but not yet rate cuts. The base case is a pause in the current cycle with rates held through the near-term horizon, pending confirmation that inflation is decelerating decisively. Any further hikes are now unlikely, but cuts are not yet warranted by the data flow.
arbitrated.falsifier: Clear disinflation signal (headline rolling below 3.5%, core below 3.0%) with labour slack accelerating would force cuts into the curve.

trade.rationale: Labour loosens modestly but inflation remains hot. Market should price a pause, not hikes or cuts. Steepen the front-end curve (short end up, 2y down) as market reprices less near-term tightening and fewer terminal hikes.
